newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwandan Hutus caught in middle of Zaire war zone.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan Hutus caught in middle of Zaire war zone.

text.p: Relief workers operating in the heart of Zaire's equatorial jungle fear for the future of up to 400,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees, sandwiched between the Zairean army and Tutsi-led rebels.

An estimated 160,000 refugees, many of them already starved and dehydrated, are in two camps on one of the few passable roads from the Zairean military headquarters in Kisangani to the rebel-occupied towns of Goma and Bukavu in the east.
With Zaire's army gearing up to launch a counter-offensive against the rebels, aid workers say satellite images reveal a further 200,000 or so refugees in inaccessible forest areas.
"Already we have serious logistical difficulties in the camp here at Tingi Tingi. If we are to give a full ration we need 63 tonnes per day," said Dr Baja Ichuma, a World Food Programme nutritionist.
"For the moment we depend on two planes and we can only bring in 24 tonnes," he added, speaking from one camp with an estimated 120,000 refugeees.

The refugees in Tingi Tingi are visibly exhausted and malnourished. Some have walked more than 500 km (300 miles) through hostile territory after fleeing rebel attacks on their camps in the Kivu border regions last November.

Children, some skeletal, others with ghost-like faces, drained by diarrhoea, sprawl in their hundreds on the floors of the medical and nutrition centres set up by the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF and Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders).
Medical workers say 10 to 20 refugees, mostly children, die of starvation or disease daily. In the past week 110 cases of cholera have been detected at Tingi Tingi alone.
On Monday the shrouded corpses of two victims were carried out of a field hospital. A young man with hollowed eyes collapsed panting on the ground on the point of death.

Over a million Hutus fled Rwanda into Zaire following the 1994 genocide there of up to a million ethnic Tutsis and Hutu moderates. Last November an estimated 600,000 of them returned home to Rwanda after rebel attacks on their border camps.

A Canadian-led multinational military force was sent under U.N. auspices to the region to help the refugees. It based itself in Uganda, achieved almost nothing and then went home after lengthy debates on how many refugees were left in Zaire.
Zaire's government has said it wants no more refugee camps on its territory.
Non-government organisations operating in the field say they cannot understand why the WFP, and UNHCR refugee agency, notably absent at the camps, lack the logistical means to help.
"I cannot understand why the WFP is not working as they can do and as they do in other parts of the world," said Bernard Jacquemart, deputy director of mission for the French NGO Medecins du Monde.
Other aid workers suggested the UNHCR had the mandate and the means to find a solution, but lacked the political will.
Tingi Tingi is 250 km (155 miles) east of the city of Kisangani, the likely springboard for the counter-offensive, and is surrounded by equatorial jungle.
Young men and all with enough strength scour the forest for roots and nuts. Women, children and the elderly have priority over scarce food rations supplied by relief agencies.

Many of the refugees said they preferred an uncertain future isolated at the heart of the Zairean jungle than to return to what they fear is certain death back home in a Rwanda whose army is now dominated by Tutsis.
"I am just waiting to die here," said a young Hutu woman. She had sold all her clothes except the rags she was wearing to buy food.
